newsitem.title: USA: CME Oct hogs end limit up, pork bellies higher.
newsitem.headline: CME Oct hogs end limit up, pork bellies higher.

text.p: CME October live hog futures closed up the 1.50-cent-per-lb daily limit and other contracts ended higher, largely on short covering after limit declines Tuesday, traders said.
Short covering carried pork bellies to higher closes as well, but gains were trimmed late when USDA midday cash belly quotes were lower than expected, traders said.

October hogs expire at 1200 CDT Thursday and analysts said it is common for the contract to expire at a premium to cash prices. October closed up 1.50 cent at 55.125 cents per lb versus $51.50 to $54.00 per cwt cash prices Wednesday in key Midwest direct trade.
Commission house LFG was featured buying October hogs near the close, while Merrill Lynch bought December, traders said.
Also, some traders said buying in hogs was largely keyed to ideas the futures became "terribly oversold" in recent sessions.

In pork bellies, traders said $1.00 to $2.00 per cwt lower cash prices in the midday USDA carlot pork price report prompted light late selling that trimmed gains. Traders had expected steady to higher pork belly prices.
Short covering in the wake of two so-called "neutral" storage reports Tuesday motivated buying in pork bellies throughout much of the day.
"In light of the break we had, you needed a negative number (to extend declines)," said one trader.

The USDA monthly Cold Storage Report showed total frozen pork supplies increased 18.3 million lbs from September 1 to October 1, but pork belly supplies decreased. USDA reported 12.68 million lbs of pork bellies in storage as of October 1, which was close to trade expectations.
Also, Tuesday's weekly CME out-of-town storage reported showed an increase of 993,000 lbs for the week, which was in line with trade expectations.
CME hogs closed up 1.50 to 0.025 cent a lb with December up 0.275 at 52.375 cents per lb. Pork bellies were up 1.075 to 0.825 cent with February up the most at 67.750.
